extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent applicants/practitioners in life sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the two-step Alice/Mayo subject‑matter eligibility framework to life‑sciences claims, including how to apply the broadest reasonable interpretation, identify closest naturally occurring counterparts, evaluate 'markedly different characteristics', and determine whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category determination (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim falls within a statutory category (e.g., process, composition of matter, machine, manufacture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a process or a composition of matter, Step 1 is satisfied (e.g., a claim reciting steps of detecting JUL-1 in plasma is a process). This is the opening statutory-category inquiry before any exception analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exception identification (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, product of nature, abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is directed to or recites a judicial exception (for example, a correlation, law of nature, or naturally occurring product), proceed to analyses of marked differences and, if necessary, Step 2B. The guidance notes that some recited steps (e.g., correlation and critical thinking) may be laws of nature or abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) to identify closest naturally occurring counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (in view of the specification) to determine the claim scope and thereby identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BRI determines whether the claim as written encompasses naturally occurring material (e.g., whether a texiol/water mixture as claimed reads on the plant sap). Use the specification's definitions where provided to limit or define BRI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (for nature-based products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claimed nature-based product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart(s) to determine whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics (structure, function, or other properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked differences can be structural, functional, organoleptic, time-release, physical form, dissolution behavior, etc. Examples include changed organoleptic properties (neutralized bitterness), altered physical form (solid gel), specific particle size distributions that change dissolution, or controlled‑release formulations. Cite Roslin and analyze whether the altered property is relevant to the nature of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify closest natural counterparts component-wise when no natural mixture exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claimed mixture or combination does not occur in nature, identify and compare the claimed components to their respective closest naturally occurring counterparts (component-wise comparisons may be necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If components do not occur together in nature, compare each component to its natural counterpart (e.g., texiol+water vs. sap, Compound N vs. its natural form) to evaluate whether the claimed combination yields markedly different characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of amounts/ratios alone insufficient for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting particular concentrations, percentages, or ratios in a claim does not automatically render a nature-based claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely claiming specific amounts (e.g., 1–5% texiol, 90% water) does not show a marked change in structure or function unless the applicant explains which characteristics are markedly different; best practice is to explain what characteristics differ and why those differences are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether any element or combination of elements beyond the judicial exception ensures that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for additional limitations that, alone or in combination, are unconventional, integrate the exception into a practical application, add meaningful limits on use, or otherwise transform the claim. Physical or tangible elements (obtaining, detecting, administering) do not automatically make a claim eligible; the totality and how those elements constrain use matter (see Alice, Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality inquiry for additional elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether recited additional elements were well‑understood, routine, and conventional in the field at the time of the invention/filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the additional steps were routine or widely prevalent, they are less likely to supply 'significantly more.' If a recited step (e.g., topical vitamin D for julitis) was not widely prevalent or routine at the time, it may be an unconventional step that contributes to eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of the exception into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a diagnostic, treatment, or other practical process so that the claim is not merely instructing practitioners to apply the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claiming a particular treatment step tied to diagnostic detection can integrate the exception into a treatment process (ensuring accurate diagnosis and proper treatment) and thus may supply 'significantly more.' The combination should meaningfully limit the claim's scope and use.

rubrics_metrics.name: New combination of known steps may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A new combination of steps in a process may confer eligibility even if all individual constituents were known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diamond v. Diehr supports that a novel combination can be patentable; examine the totality of steps and whether the combination yields meaningful limits or practical application beyond the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangible/physical elements alone do not automatically confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere recitation of physical, tangible steps or items (e.g., obtaining a sample, detecting a protein, administering a drug) does not by itself ensure eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether those tangible elements, considered alone or in combination, add meaningful limits or are merely routine activities that apply the exception using well-understood techniques. Cite Alice/Alice Corp. and Mayo as authority that physicality alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection/allowance record guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Office actions and reasons for allowance should explain the basis for concluding that a claim is directed to an exception or is eligible, and should identify the exception(s) and closest natural counterpart(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection should point to the nature‑based product or other exception in the claim and explain why it lacks markedly different characteristics or why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. If helpful, cite analogous court decisions (e.g., Roslin, Funk Brothers, Myriad, Diehr, Mayo). If the claim is eligible, the record may note that the exception exists but the claim recites additional limitations that are unconventional or integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Step 2B need not be performed
rubrics_metrics.description: If analysis under Step 2A concludes the claim is not directed to any judicial exception (i.e., the claim has no exception or has markedly different characteristics), Step 2B is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Step 2A resolves eligibility in favor of the claim, examiners need not perform the Step 2B 'significantly more' analysis. The record may nevertheless include explanatory remarks for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analogous case law for explanatory support
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a rejection or allowance, examiners may cite analogous court decisions to illustrate why a claimed invention is or is not like a judicially excluded category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Roslin (cloned mammals), Funk Brothers (bacterial mixtures), Myriad (products of nature), Diehr (combinations), Mayo/Alice (laws of nature/abstract ideas). Use analogies to explain lack of marked changes or to support why combination/limitations supply significantly more.
